newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Tullow plans intensive exploration programme.
newsitem.headline: Tullow plans intensive exploration programme.

text.p: Irish oil and gas producer and explorer Tullow Oil Plc said on Friday that it had the resources to fund an aggressive exploration programme, develop existing discoveries and expand into new areas.
Tullow said in a statement its exploration programme was currently being expanded into some promising new areas, with licences currently being finalised in India and Bangladesh.

"Activity in the company over the next 12 months will be intense with exploration, development and production projects spread between established countries and new areas," managing director Aidan Heavey said.

Earlier, Tullow said its pre-tax profit for the six months to June 30, 1996, had increased by 43 percent to 1.2 million Irish pounds. The company said its financial position had been greatly strengthened by the placing of a $10 million loan note in March and a one-for-five rights issue which had raised 30.3 million pounds sterling in August.
"The strong support for the rights issue earlier this year has provided a sound platform for developing the company's asset base," Heavey said.
Tullow said considerable emphasis had been placed on expanding its asset base in order to give a better geographical spread and allow for greater growth.
"By the end of 1996, we expect to have one new exploration licence in Egypt and two in Bangladesh, while contract negotiations on two Indian blocks should be underway," Heavey said.
Tullow said futher development and exploration licences had been applied for or are being evaluated in a number of countries.
The company said the results of its drilling programme for 1996 in Pakistan had been disappointing in comparison to its previous excellent success rate.

"The first appraisal well on the Sara discovery, while proving the areal extent of the reservoir sand, was beyond the margin of the field. The second well, on the other side of a fault, proved water wet," Heavey said.

"This has downgraded our estimate of reserves for the Sara field. The faulting in the area proved to be more complicated than expected and it is more likely that a number of individual shallow structures exist," he added.
Tullow said it was planning a drilling programme for 1997 to target thse structures which should prove up further reserves in line with its original expecatations.
In the meantime, Tullow said it had requested approval from the Pakistani government to sell the Sara gas to the local power station while awaiting construction of the Liberty Power Plant.
This early production, while giving a valuable cash flow and profit, would help in quantifying the size of the reserves, it said.

Tullow said it had commissioned a feasibility study to examine the possibility of commercially developing its exploration well in Block B, Sara West 1, in light of the high flow rates, pressure and the size of the structure.
It said a further development well, West Firsby 6, in the UK was currently being drilled and, if successful, would enhance oil production from the West Firsby field.
Tullow said it expected first oil sales from its Kishma field in Syria in March/April 1996. It said the appraisal well, Kishma 2, due to be spudded in late 1996, might add to this production.
